summary:
Serbia does not criminalise consensual same-sex activity or transgender identity. Male homosexual intercourse was decriminalised in 1994 through an amendment to article 110 of the Criminal Code, and since 1 January 2006 the Criminal Code has set an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. The Anti-Discrimination Act approved on 26 March 2009 prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and transgender status in all areas, and amendments in 2021 added sex characteristics. A Penal Code hate-crime provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted on 24 December 2012; the first conviction followed in 2018 and enforcement remains weak.

No form of legal recognition exists for same-sex couples. Article 62 of the Constitution adopted in November 2006 defines marriage as entered into on the free consent of a man and a woman, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt or access the legal protections available to opposite-sex households. A draft domestic partnership law announced in June 2019 covered joint property and alimony but not inheritance, adoption or surrogacy; a Novi Sad couple were turned away when they tried to register a civil partnership in July 2019 and sued, with legal experts doubting they would win. A further draft reached public consultation in February 2021, but President Aleksandar Vučić said in May 2021 he would not sign it as unconstitutional, the bill stalled without a vote, and he reaffirmed in August 2023 that he would sign no such law during his term. The Green-Left Front submitted a new Draft Law on Civil Partnership in September 2024 covering maintenance, inheritance and health and social insurance; it remains unscheduled for a vote. The 2023 Grand Chamber ruling of the European Court of Human Rights in Fedotova and Others v. Russia holds that Council of Europe states, Serbia included, have a positive obligation to provide some form of legal recognition for same-sex couples.

Police conduct is the sharpest documented exposure. In February 2024 Serbian authorities opened an investigation into allegations that officers assaulted, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during an apartment raid in Belgrade; no sanction against officers has been reported.

Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records that intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns in Serbia during 2024, and that the state response to the July and August protests, including activist arrests and smear campaigns, highlighted rule-of-law weaknesses.

Civil-society infrastructure has been directly targeted. The Pride Info Centre was attacked in January 2024 and announced its closure in September after more than 20 attacks since 2018, none of which was properly sanctioned.

Public assembly has a long record of state failure to protect. The first Belgrade Pride in 2001 ended in extreme violence, and Pride events in Belgrade in 2004 and 2009 and in Novi Sad in 2007 were cancelled because police could not guarantee safety against violent opponents. The 2010 Belgrade Pride went ahead with about a thousand participants and was met by a riot attended by 6,000 anti-gay protesters and members of extreme nationalist groups. Belgrade Pride has been held annually since September 2014, except in 2020 when it moved online for COVID-19. EuroPride in September 2022 was initially banned on security grounds and opposed by President Vučić but proceeded on 17 September along a shortened route under heavy police protection, with organisers reporting almost 10,000 attendees. Novi Sad held its first pride rally on 17 May 2019.

For trans people in custody, the Association for the Prevention of Torture records a national preventive mechanism recommendation that the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela, Belgrade, allow transgender women at intake to choose a female officer for searches and body inspection rather than a male or combined search.

Healthcare access is partial. Sex change surgeries have been partially covered by the state basic medical insurance since a Health Insurance Act change approved on 28 July 2011 and effective in 2012, with insurance covering up to 65% of surgery costs and the patient paying the remainder; hormone replacement therapy is not financed by health insurance. ILGA-Europe's 2025 annual review records testosterone supply shortages affecting trans people.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Map ranked Serbia 29th of 49 European countries with a 34% score, down from 27th in 2024.
tangentialFactors:
A publication analysed 70 instances of politicians' hate speech in Serbia between April 2023 and April 2024.

The US State Department's 2018 human rights report for Serbia listed violence targeting LGBTI individuals among the country's human rights problems, alongside government corruption and violence against journalists.

The Ministry of Health barred people with a documented history of homosexual relations during the preceding five years from donating reproductive cells for artificial insemination or IVF in early 2019; the provision was removed on 23 April 2021.

Official medical textbooks circulated in Serbia classifying homosexuality under sexual deviations and disorders until the Serbian Medical Society confirmed in a 2008 letter to the advocacy group Labris that same-sex orientation is not a disease; homosexuality had been removed from the official disease list in 1997 under ICD-10.

Belgrade was described by The New York Times in 2012 as a hub for sex reassignment surgery because prices were far lower than in neighbouring and Western countries.

Earlier criminalisation stages: the 1860 Penalty Act of the Principality punished intercourse against the order of nature between males with six months to four years' imprisonment and did not mention lesbian sexuality; the 1929 Yugoslav Criminal Code banned lewdness against the order of nature between heterosexuals and homosexuals alike; the SFRY narrowed the offence in 1959 to homosexual anal intercourse with the maximum cut from two years to one. Same-sex intercourse was legalised in Vojvodina in 1977 but male homosexuality was re-criminalised when Vojvodina was reincorporated into Serbia's legal system in 1990. The 1994 decriminalisation left a subsection banning male same-sex acts for males aged 14 to 18 with up to one year's prison, which the 2006 Criminal Code removed.

The civil-society group Da se zna! presented its eighth annual hate-crime report, Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024, on 2 September 2025; it is the standing civil-society incident register for the year.
localsOnly:
A survey conducted by Zoomer found that three-quarters of trans and non-binary people in Serbia fear job interviews because of anticipated discrimination.

A reported 90% of LGBT individuals in Serbia say medical institutions are not adequately responding to their needs, and Jovanka Todorović of Gayten-LGBT said about 80% of Serbian transgender people are not willing to undergo surgery.

Public opinion is split. 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data shows 26% support for same-sex marriage but 80% believing LGBTI+ persons should have at least some of the rights in a same-sex union law, second-highest in the Western Balkans after Montenegro; 2018 data cited by the US State Department shows 70% opposing an LGBT person inheriting a deceased partner's property.

Attitudes toward LGBT young people and parenting remain hostile: 2018 data cited in the US State Department human rights report found 48% of parents would seek medical treatment for their LGBT child and 90% opposed child adoption by an LGBT person, while a 2022 World Values Survey found 65% of Serbians disagreed that homosexual couples are as good parents as other couples.

Support is markedly higher among respondents aged 18 to 29 and among university-educated respondents in Belgrade and Vojvodina, and 2021 Civil Rights Defenders data records a general improvement in attitudes toward LGBTI+ issues over the preceding five years, though 57% still believe homosexuality is a disease.
outOfScopeNotes:
The February 2024 investigation into the alleged assault, torture and sexual harassment of two LGBT people by police in Belgrade has no reported outcome or sanction; whether it produced charges is unresolved.

Beyond the first hate-crime conviction in 2018, the number of prosecutions or convictions under the 2012 Penal Code hate-crime provision is not sourced.

The content of the Da se zna! 2024 hate-crime register, including incident counts and categories, is not detailed in the available material.

Whether Serbia has taken any legislative step toward the legal recognition of same-sex couples in response to the 2023 Fedotova and Others v. Russia ruling is not sourced.
